subject: Career
title: Building Coalitions for Change
description: A quick, practical guide to Building Coalitions for Change.

hook.text: One person proposing change is a complaint. Five people proposing change is a movement.

buildup.text: Coalitions amplify your voice. Gathering supporters before proposing shows the idea has broad backing.

discovery.text: John Kotter's research: 75% of organizational change fails. The #1 reason? Not building enough coalition first.

twist.text: Coalitions need diverse members: people with authority, people with expertise, and people with influence.

climax.text: Before the big meeting, have one-on-ones. Get buy-in privately. The meeting becomes a formality.

punchline.text: Win the room before you enter it.

quiz.question: What is the #1 reason organizational change fails according to Kotter?

details.summary: Coalitions are temporary alliances of individuals united around a specific goal or change initiative. Building an effective coalition requires identifying stakeholders, understanding their interests, and framing the change in terms that resonate with each group.
details.whyItMatters: Individual advocacy rarely moves organizations. Coalitions create the critical mass of support needed to overcome institutional inertia and resistance to change.
takeaways: Map stakeholders into supporters, opponents, and persuadables
Frame the same initiative differently for each stakeholder group
Start with easy wins to build coalition momentum and credibility

faq.question: How many people do you need in a coalition to create organizational change?
faq.answer: Research suggests you need roughly twenty-five percent of an organization to adopt a new behavior before it tips to majority adoption. For internal initiatives, winning over three to five influential stakeholders often provides enough momentum to move forward.

faq.question: What do you do when coalition members have conflicting interests?
faq.answer: Focus on the shared goal that unites them and allow flexibility on implementation details. Effective coalitions do not require agreement on everything. They require agreement on the core objective and tolerance for differences on peripheral issues.
